N° 10Interactive lab on Cameroon's Internet2026

Lemon Connect Cameroon

Why is the Internet slow and expensive in Cameroon, and what would make it better? A lab where visitors follow a packet from a phone in Douala to a server, cause network faults and repair them, see who is responsible for what, and test market reforms, with every fact dated and sourced.

Visit the site ↗How to useIn motion

01

Problem

Most people in Cameroon live with slow and costly connections without knowing where the problem sits: the antenna, the power supply, the backbone, the international link or the market itself. Public debate often blames one actor without evidence, and the data that exists is scattered across reports in two languages.

02

What it does

The site turns the network into experiments. On the home page, a request from a phone in Douala crosses every piece of equipment, each one clickable, and visitors can cause congestion, a power cut or a fibre cut and watch speed and delay change. A 4G and 5G lab finds the bottleneck in a cell; a fault lab holds 16 incidents, from batteries to BGP, where the wrong repair is shown to fail. Other modules map who is responsible for what in technical, contractual and regulatory terms, model the market with nine scenarios and a two-operator game, compare satellite and ground links, size an installation for Lemon Network Solutions, build an operator over five years, and set out a roadmap for ART and MINPOSTEL. An observatory, an academy of ten courses, an atlas of cables and CAMIX, and a sources page complete it. A welcome screen offers four paths, each page has a guided tour, and 139 technical terms show their definition on hover or tap.

03

How it is built

React and TypeScript with Vite and Tailwind, hosted on Vercel. The simulations run on a small engine written in TypeScript and tested on its own: radio capacity from the 3GPP model, queues, fibre delay, power availability, a market model with fixed costs, a game between operators and a five-year finance model. Facts live in two research files with more than 100 dated sources, and each figure on screen carries its reference. 52 unit tests check the engine and 54 browser tests walk through the site on a computer and an Android phone.
